results.corrected_extracted: The coronary thrombosis death rate in smokers was no more than twice that of non-smokers, possibly less; though there is good evidence to support causation, Hill finds it much easier in this case to think of features of life going hand in hand with smoking, such as lack of exercise or diet, that might conceivably be the real underlying cause or at least an important contributor; the lung cancer death rate, nine to ten times that of non-smokers (p. 295), would need a feature so closely tied to smoking and to the amount smoked that it should be easy to detect.
results.note: Place right. The anchor dropped Hill's qualifier 'Though there is good evidence to support causation' (for coronary thrombosis too) and the hedge 'conceivably ... at the least'; restored.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors found relationships between drug use in and after Vietnam and later problems (excessive drinking, arrests, unemployment, depression, psychiatric care), yet say they could not necessarily assume the drug use caused them: factors before the drug use may have led both to the use and to the problems, and problems after return may have led men back to narcotics. Without a sample that included men who had not served in Vietnam, they add, they cannot tell whether these problems were more frequent than expected. After further analyses, including a multivariate one in which drug use competed with predictors such as school completion, broken home and arrests before service, they say the results suggest that drug use in and before Vietnam was indeed a powerful factor in poor adjustment after return, but that its effects were contingent on continuing drug use after Vietnam (p. 960).
results.corrected_locator: Results › Drug Use and Post-Vietnam Adjustment, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 959, left column, continuing in the right column) and paragraph beginning 'To examine whether' (p. 960, left column)
results.note: The p. 959 passage is rendered right (restored 'not necessarily assume'), but on p. 960 the authors go on to their own conclusion on this question; leaving it out makes their view look more agnostic than it is.

results.corrected_extracted: In the principal investigator's account, heroin went with more adverse outcomes (crime, unemployment, divorce or separation, violence, alcohol and drug problems and others) than amphetamines or barbiturates, but not once behaviour problems before service and the number of other kinds of drugs used were held constant: then the other drugs went with as many problems, and the variety of drugs used predicted problems better than which drugs. results.corrected_extracted: Citing a content analysis of high-profile news coverage of research presented at five scientific meetings (Woloshin & Schwartz, 2006b), the authors report that few stories included cautions about studies with inherent limitations: for example, only 10% of stories about uncontrolled studies noted that it was impossible to know whether the outcome really related to the exposure. results.note: 10% and the wording confirmed (pp. 66-67). 'No sample size given' is not right: Table 6 lists Woloshin & Schwartz 2006b with n = 187; only the uncontrolled-study denominator is missing.

results.corrected_extracted: For several diseases, including alcoholism and opiate addiction (the paper's terms), clinicians sample the people ill at a given moment (a prevalence or census sample), which is biased toward long-lasting cases because each case's chance of being in it is proportional to how long it lasts, whereas research samples tend to come closer to everyone who ever develops the condition; the authors call this bias the clinician's illusion, and say part of the disagreement about long-term prognosis may be attributable to this difference in the populations sampled.
results.note: Abstract, p. 1178. The abstract says 'research samples tend to more nearly represent', not 'follow-up research comes closer'; restored 'tend to' and the hedge 'Part of this disagreement may be attributable'.

p. 1181: 1st paragraph (useful when conclusions are limited to patients seen in services like the source) and 11th paragraph (without careful specification of treatment history and selection, the population is unknown).

results.corrected_extracted: The author calls the Vietnam situation one unknown before: never had so many young men been addicted to opiates without the usual risk factors, and few would have become addicted had they stayed in the US. Yet in the same paragraph he says he thinks the results were both correct and not unique: the men's brief addiction followed by spontaneous recovery, in Vietnam and afterwards, was out of line only with American beliefs, not with American experience, and their ability to use again without becoming re-addicted was not very unusual.
results.note: Place right (p. 1051). The paragraph's point is 'the results were both correct and not unique'; quoting only the 'unknown situation' half reverses the author's conclusion, so his counterpoint is added.

results.corrected_extracted: Hill's temporality viewpoint: which came first. His examples: a diet may lead to a disease, or the early stages of the disease may lead to the diet; a job may promote tuberculosis, or the people who choose that work may be more liable to it or already infected. He calls the question particularly relevant to diseases of slow development, and says this temporal problem may not arise often but certainly needs to be remembered, particularly with selective factors at work in industry.
results.note: Place right (pp. 297-298). Restored Hill's hedge that the temporal problem 'may not arise often' and his scope (diseases of slow development; selective factors in industry).

results.corrected_extracted: Running many analyses and reporting only those with certain p-values (typically those passing a significance threshold) makes the reported p-values essentially uninterpretable, and cherry-picking promising findings leads to a spurious excess of statistically significant results in the published literature; researchers should disclose the number of hypotheses explored, all data collection decisions, all statistical analyses conducted and all p-values computed.
results.note: Place right (pp. 131-132, principle 4). The statement asks to disclose 'the number of hypotheses explored', not every hypothesis, and also 'all data collection decisions'.

p. 296, right column, (2) Consistency, 1st-3rd paragraphs: 29 retrospective and 7 prospective inquiries (found by the Surgeon-General's Advisory Committee); 'not due to some constant error or fallacy that permeates every inquiry'.

results.corrected_extracted: Repetition has limits: a bias built into a design is not removed, and not necessarily revealed, by any number of exact repetitions (Heady's hospital example); the same results from precisely the same form of inquiry will not invariably greatly strengthen the original evidence, while Hill puts a good deal of weight on similar results reached in quite different ways; and where repetition is absent or impossible a unique observation can still convince (South Wales nickel refiners, 1929-1938: 16 lung cancer deaths against about one expected, 11 nasal cancer deaths against a fraction of one).
results.note: Place right (pp. 296-297). Hill: repetitions 'would remove or necessarily reveal' nothing, i.e. not necessarily revealed (the anchor said never revealed); 'add less' replaced by his hedge 'will not invariably greatly strengthen'. Numbers confirmed.
pp. 2-3: title and first two sentences for press releases and news ('inverted pyramid'); abstract and discussion for journal articles.

results.corrected_extracted: Of 462 health press releases from 20 UK universities in 2011, measured against the journal article, 40% (95% CI 33% to 46%) of 213 gave more direct or explicit advice, 33% (26% to 40%) of 182 stated correlational results more causally, and 36% (28% to 46%) of 105 on studies in animals, cells or simulations stretched the results to humans; the authors say these levels are likely to be underestimates, given the likelihood that other scientists in the specialty would consider some statements in the journal articles themselves exaggerated.
results.note: All numbers and denominators confirmed (pp. 2-3). Only the reason for 'underestimates' was firmer than the source: 'some articles themselves overstate' replaced by the authors' 'would be considered exaggerated by other scientists'.
